rationale: A wins because its lanes are cleaner and the disclosure angle is a real reporter question, not a padded restatement of the store rollout. “Warby Parker says it’s profitable — but won’t say how much comes from eye exams” turns the missing number into a story; B’s “the historically defensible, insurance-tied part of the optical business the incumbents have owned” may be true, but it is imported scaffolding, not in the update. Both sets are usable, but A asks the founder to prove the supplied facts, while B asks them to defend a little too much outside industry lore.
gaps_in_A: “Warby Parker is testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores” overclaims the pilot. The facts say pharmacy-chain sales are being tested, not that Warby is comparing the channel against its own stores.
“Warby Parker bets its future on the stores it was built to disrupt” is a sharp frame, but “bets its future” is too grand for a 40-store expansion unless the company can prove strategic dependence.
“CVS-MinuteClinic-style trend” imports an outside comparison without supplied proof. It works as a beat cue, but it should stay out of the pitch unless supported.

The next step jumps to journalist-fit-check before saying the founder must fill the pharmacy partner name and retail-spend multiplier. Those are not nice-to-haves; they decide whether two angles survive first contact.
gaps_in_B: “the historically defensible, insurance-tied part of the optical business the incumbents have owned” is plausible trade analysis, but it is not in the provided facts. This is where smart-sounding copy starts writing checks the fact sheet cannot cash.
“The store that costs more to build is the one Warby says pays off” assumes store-level cost structure and capex economics not provided in the update. Obvious does not mean sourced.
Angle 1 and angle 3 both ride the same optometrist-staffed-store fact. The competitive lens and retail-health lens are different enough to keep, but the set is less cleanly distinct than it thinks.
“exam upsell” nudges toward an unproven revenue story even while the set correctly says exam revenue is not broken out. Do not smuggle the conclusion into the question.
